details:
GeoQocha is an interactive, open-source web dashboard that analyzes the socio-environmental conditions of the 15 municipal districts of Cochabamba, Bolivia. The project combines NASA satellite data—primarily NDVI to assess vegetation and LST to analyze surface temperature—with territorial information from the Autonomous Municipal Government of Cochabamba (GAMC). The data covers the period 2015–2025 and is presented through maps, graphs, inter-district comparisons, trends, hotspots, and a socio-environmental quality-of-life index.

The platform helps identify environmental changes, territorial inequalities, and areas requiring greater attention. Its benefits include facilitating access to scientific information, supporting data-driven decision-making, promoting environmental education, and helping authorities, researchers, and citizens understand how their territory is evolving.

The expected impact of GeoQocha is to contribute to more informed urban and environmental planning, strengthening Cochabamba’s capacity to detect risks, prioritize interventions, and assess its socio-environmental conditions over time. The project also aims to make Earth observation data more accessible to the public through a clear and understandable interface.

React, Vite, and TypeScript were used on the front end to develop GeoQocha, while Node.js with Express and TypeScript were used on the back end. Python and/or Google Earth Engine are also used for data processing, along with Leaflet for maps and Recharts for visualizations. The information is organized into JSON and GeoJSON files, using data from NASA’s MODIS products and municipal territorial layers. The system includes a limited artificial intelligence “co-pilot,” designed to explain pre-calculated results without fabricating figures or replacing scientific analysis.

The project’s innovation lies in integrating satellite observation, municipal data, geographic visualization, and artificial intelligence into a tool specifically focused on the reality of Cochabamba. The team considered data quality and availability, differences between districts, source transparency, privacy and security of credentials, interface accessibility, limitations of historical data, and the need to clearly distinguish between actual information and illustrative examples.
